name: Epistane (Epitiostanol-derivative, Havoc)

card.summary: An oral designer steroid once sold as a supplement; case reports link it to liver bile-flow problems and nobody has trialled it.
card.note: Controlled steroid in the US since 2014; prohibited in sport; cholestasis case reports.

quick.overview:
Epistane is an oral anabolic steroid related to epitiostanol, a Japanese breast-cancer drug. It was never approved, but began appearing in online muscle supplements around 2009.

No clinical trials have tested it for muscle or appearance. What exists in the literature is chemical analysis of products and a small set of case reports.
quick.mechanism: It is a 17alpha-methylated androgen from the DHT family. Laboratory work on human liver cells suggests it increases bile acid synthesis and interacts with nuclear receptors.
quick.risks: A 2020 case series reported prolonged cholestasis in four users. Its 17alpha-methyl group is associated with liver toxicity. It is a controlled steroid in the US since 2014 and is prohibited by WADA.

lead: Epistane, also called methylepitiostanol, 17alpha-methylepithiostanol, Havoc, Hemapolin or Epi Plex, is a synthetic, orally active anabolic-androgenic steroid of the dihydrotestosterone (DHT) group, derived from epitiostanol, a compound used in Japan in breast cancer treatment.[1][2][3] It was never marketed as a medicine, but it has been sold online as a 'prohormone'-style bodybuilding supplement since about 2009, aimed at users who want more muscle and a harder, drier look.[2][3]

Wikipedia classifies it as an androgen, anabolic steroid and antiestrogen, and describes it as having a high potential for liver toxicity because of its 17alpha-methyl group.[3] Analytical chemists found it in over-the-counter products around 2009, with some products also containing desoxymethyltestosterone, and a later review identified it in more than 30 online products that listed it as an ingredient.[2][3] Epistane is on the World Anti-Doping Agency prohibited list and has been a controlled substance in the United States since 2014.[2][3]

No controlled trials in healthy users have been published. The main human data are case reports: a 2020 toxicology study described four people who developed long-lasting cholestasis after taking it.[1]

chain: Claimed gains in lean mass and a drier look
angle.text: Supplement sellers and some bodybuilders present epistane as an oral way to add lean mass and a dry, hard appearance. These claims come from marketing and community reports; no trial has measured them, and the documented human data concern liver effects.

infobox: US controlled substance since 2014 (Schedule III); WADA-prohibited[2][3]

paras: Epistane is a 17alpha-methyl derivative of epitiostanol with a 2alpha,3alpha-epithio ring, and is closely related to mepitiostane. Its formula is C20H32OS and its molar mass is about 320.5 g/mol.[3] One analytical paper noted it may act as a prodrug of desoxymethyltestosterone, and analysis of supplements found a different epithio isomer and desoxymethyltestosterone in an Epistane-labelled product.[2]

The compound was first described in the literature in 1974 by Miyake and colleagues and was never developed as a drug.[3] It appeared in dietary supplements around 2009 under names such as Epistane and P-Plex; analysts examining two products obtained online reported that both contained ingredients prohibited in sport, and that the labels did not always match the contents.[2] By 2015 it was found in more than 30 online products listing it as an ingredient.[3] In 2014 the US Designer Anabolic Steroid Control Act added it to the controlled list among 27 new steroids.[3]

Wikipedia lists epistane as an androgen receptor agonist with antiestrogenic properties, in the DHT group of steroids.[3] A 2020 laboratory study in human liver cells reported that it upregulates bile acid synthesis through the enzyme CYP8B1 and interacts with nuclear receptors.[1]

Wikipedia notes that its 17alpha-methyl group is associated with a high potential for liver toxicity.[3] The 2020 study in Archives of Toxicology described four individuals who developed prolonged cholestasis after consuming epistane; in three of them serum bile acids were raised 14- to 61-fold, and cell experiments supported a mechanism through bile acid synthesis.[1]
Epistane was sold as a supplement ingredient for muscle gain, often in 'prohormone' style products. It is prohibited in sport, and US law has treated it as a controlled steroid since 2014.[2][3]
No controlled clinical trials have been published. Human evidence is limited to a case series of four people with cholestasis after use.[1]
